cores.title: From atomic balance to reversibility
assumptions: The state space is countable, carries a measurable space, and every singleton is measurable.
\(\mu\) is a nonnegative measure and \(K\) is a measurable kernel; neither is assumed finite or normalized.
For every pair \(x,y\), \(\mu(\{x\})K(x,\{y\})=\mu(\{y\})K(y,\{x\})\) in the extended nonnegative reals.
cores.question: Prove that for all measurable sets A,B, \(\int_A K(x,B)\,d\mu(x)=\int_B K(y,A)\,d\mu(y)\). Explain why infinite total mass and zero-mass states cause no cancellation problem. Does this imply convergence to a probability law?
steps: On a countable measurable-singleton space, expand each restricted integral and each kernel mass into singleton masses. The left side becomes \[\sum_{x\in A}\sum_{y\in B}K(x,\{y\})\mu(\{x\}).\] These sums take values in \([0,\infty]\).

Apply the assumed balance identity to each summand. Nonnegativity permits exchanging the two sums even when the result is infinite: \[\sum_{x\in A}\sum_{y\in B}\mu(\{y\})K(y,\{x\})=\sum_{y\in B}K(y,A)\mu(\{y\}).\]

Recognize the last expression as the right restricted integral. No division by a singleton mass, subtraction of infinities, or signed Fubini argument occurred. A zero atom needs no special conditional version for this flux identity.
Reversibility alone proves neither normalization, irreducibility, convergence, nor a mixing or query-cost bound. Those require separate assumptions and arguments.

rubric.criterion: States the countability and measurable-singleton hypotheses and uses nonnegative extended-valued sums.
Expands both the outer restricted integral and the inner kernel mass.
Uses balance termwise and justifies sum exchange without dividing by masses or subtracting infinities.
Separates reversibility from normalization, convergence and computational cost.

cores.title: PL descent: the sign of the contraction factor
assumptions: \(E\) is a complete real inner-product space, \(f:E\to\mathbb R\), and \(z\) is an attained global minimizer.
The real parameters \(\alpha,\beta,h\) satisfy \(h\ge0\) and \(\beta h\le1\). For all \(x,y\), the quadratic upper model holds: \[f(y)\le f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\tfrac\beta2\|y-x\|^2.\]

For every \(x\), \(2\alpha(f(x)-f(z))\le\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\). Here \(\nabla f\) is the representing vector of the derivative where \(f\) is Fréchet differentiable, and zero otherwise. The upper-model and PL inequalities are supplied assumptions; global differentiability is not inferred from the notation.
cores.question: For the actual iterates \(x_{n+1}=x_n-h\nabla f(x_n)\), prove \(f(x_N)-f(z)\le(1-\alpha h)^N(f(x_0)-f(z))\). Do not add convexity or assume \(1-\alpha h\ge0\). Explain separately what happens when this factor is negative, and when the bound describes genuine geometric decay.
steps: Substitute the actual gradient step into the quadratic model. Using \(h\ge0\) and \(\beta h\le1\) yields \[f(x-h\nabla f(x))\le f(x)-\tfrac h2\|\nabla f(x)\|^2.\]
Multiply the PL bound by h/2≥0. With \(g(x)=f(x)-f(z)\ge0\) and \(q=1-\alpha h\), obtain \(0\le g(x-h\nabla f(x))\le qg(x)\).
If q≥0, multiplication preserves order. Induction along the actual iterates gives \(g(x_N)\le q^N g(x_0)\), including N=0.

If q<0, the same one-step inequality holds for every x and forces g(x)=0: otherwise qg(x)<0 contradicts nonnegativity of the next gap. Hence every gap is zero and the displayed bound still holds. Nontrivial geometric decay requires \(0\le q<1\), rather than merely the existence of a real power q^N.

rubric.criterion: Derives the descent estimate from the actual update and the supplied quadratic model.
Uses nonnegative h/2 to combine PL with descent and obtains a nonnegative gap recurrence.
Proves the iteration bound for q≥0 and handles q<0 by showing every gap vanishes.
Does not add convexity or a hidden sign premise; distinguishes a bound from strict geometric decay.

cores.title: A quadratic envelope from one midpoint
assumptions: \(E\) is a real normed vector space; \(V:E\to\mathbb R\); \(x_0\) is an attained global minimizer; \(k\) is real.
Use the following strong-convexity convention (also used by Mathlib): on all of \(E\), for \(a,b\ge0\) with \(a+b=1\), \[V(ax+by)\le aV(x)+bV(y)-\tfrac k2 ab\|x-y\|^2.\]
No differentiability or finite-dimensionality assumption is made.
cores.question: Use only the midpoint instance and global minimality to prove \(V(x)\ge V(x_0)+\tfrac k4\|x-x_0\|^2\) for every x. Track the constant. Does this proof establish the sharper k/2 envelope, or finiteness of a Gibbs normalizer?
steps: At \(m=(x_0+x)/2\), strong convexity gives \[V(m)\le\tfrac12V(x_0)+\tfrac12V(x)-\tfrac k8\|x-x_0\|^2.\] The factor \(k/8\) comes from \((k/2)(1/2)(1/2)\).
Global minimality gives \(V(x_0)\le V(m)\). Combine the two inequalities and multiply by 2 to obtain \(V(x_0)+\tfrac k4\|x-x_0\|^2\le V(x)\). No derivative or limit was used.
This midpoint calculation proves the k/4 envelope, not the sharper k/2 constant. Obtaining a sharper result needs another argument; it must not be credited to this calculation.

The envelope alone is not a normalization theorem. One sufficient route assumes k>0, a finite-dimensional Euclidean space with Lebesgue reference measure and measurable V, then compares exp(−V) with an integrable Gaussian and separately checks positivity of the normalizer. These are conditions for that route, not necessary conditions for every Gibbs normalization: on ℝ, V(x)=|x| is convex with k=0 and exp(−|x|) has integral 2.

rubric.criterion: States the convention and obtains the midpoint correction k/8 exactly.
Uses the exposed global minimizer at the midpoint.

Separates the quadratic envelope from Gibbs integrability and normalization.

cores.title: Wasserstein symmetry without an optimal plan
assumptions: Let E be a finite-dimensional real Euclidean space with its Borel sigma-algebra. Let μ,ν be probability measures with finite second moments.
A coupling γ has marginals μ,ν. Define W₂(μ,ν) as the infimum of the square root of ∫‖x−y‖² dγ over such couplings. Do not assume an infimizing coupling is attained.
cores.question: Prove symmetry of W₂ by swapping coordinates of near-optimal couplings. Which measurability and marginal identities are used, and where does the finite-cost hypothesis prevent an invalid subtraction of infinities?
steps: The coordinate swap S(x,y)=(y,x) is continuous and hence Borel measurable. For γ′=S#γ, the identities π₁∘S=π₂ and π₂∘S=π₁ give marginals ν,μ by composition of pushforwards.
Nonnegative change of variables and symmetry of the norm give \[\int\|x-y\|^2\,d(S_\#\gamma)=\int\|y-x\|^2\,d\gamma=\int\|x-y\|^2\,d\gamma.\] No signed Fubini theorem is required.

The product coupling has finite quadratic cost since ‖x−y‖²≤2‖x‖²+2‖y‖². Thus the infimum is finite and, for each ε>0, an admissible coupling can be selected with square-root cost less than W₂(μ,ν)+ε. This is near-optimal selection, not an optimal-plan existence theorem.

Swapping this plan gives W₂(ν,μ)≤W₂(μ,ν)+ε. Let ε decrease to zero, then interchange μ and ν to obtain equality. Finiteness justifies the real-valued ε argument; there was no operation ∞−∞. The library also treats an extended-valued generalization, which is not silently identified with this question.

rubric.criterion: Checks swap measurability and both pushforward marginal identities.
Proves nonnegative quadratic-cost preservation.
Supplies finite product-coupling cost and near-optimal selection rather than assuming attainment.
Passes ε to zero in both directions without subtracting infinities.

cores.title: Why a sphere gradient is a projected ambient gradient
assumptions: E,H are real Hilbert spaces. F:E→H is Fréchet differentiable at w, with bounded linear derivative D(w). Fix r∈H and V(w)=2⟨r,F(w)⟩.
Assume ‖w‖=1 and ‖D(w)‖≤M with M≥0. The tangent space of the unit sphere at w is {v:⟨w,v⟩=0}.
cores.question: Set g=2D(w)*r and G=g−⟨g,w⟩w. Prove tangency, the directional-derivative identity on tangent vectors and ‖G‖≤2M‖r‖. Explain precisely why the same formula need not project onto w-perpendicular when w is not a unit vector.
steps: The chain rule and the adjoint identity give DV(w)[v]=2⟨r,D(w)v⟩=⟨g,v⟩. This uses genuine differentiability, not an assertion about a default derivative value.
Since ‖w‖²=1, \[\langle w,G\rangle=\langle w,g\rangle-\langle g,w\rangle\|w\|^2=0.\] For v perpendicular to w, ⟨G,v⟩=⟨g,v⟩=DV(w)[v], which identifies the sphere gradient by the induced metric.
The Pythagorean calculation gives ‖G‖²=‖g‖²−⟨g,w⟩²≤‖g‖². Hence ‖G‖≤‖g‖≤2‖D(w)*‖‖r‖=2‖D(w)‖‖r‖≤2M‖r‖.

Without normalization, ⟨w,G⟩=⟨g,w⟩(1−‖w‖²). For example, take E=ℝ, w=2 and g=2: G=−6 is not perpendicular to w. For a nonzero general normal, the projector instead divides the coefficient by ‖w‖². This is not a formula for an arbitrary manifold without its own tangent and metric data.

rubric.criterion: Derives the ambient derivative using the chain rule and adjoint, with genuine differentiability.
Uses the unit-normal condition to prove tangency and the tangent directional identity.

cores.title: Null atoms in a random-scan balance proof
assumptions: μ is any probability measure on the finite Boolean cube with n+1 coordinates. K is its uniform random-site heat-bath kernel, with the project's fixed conditional versions at null fibers.

At any start y with μ({y})>0, the exact singleton transition formula is the sum over coordinates of the retained-coordinate indicator times μ({x}) divided by the corresponding fiber mass, averaged by 1/(n+1). No such formula is assumed at an unsupported start.
cores.question: In the detailed-balance proof, handle a target-null atom x without applying the positive-start singleton formula at x. Why is zero mass alone insufficient for an arbitrary kernel? Give a reversible heat-bath example which is not irreducible.
steps: If μ({x})=μ({y})=0, both weighted transition masses vanish: finite Markov transition masses make multiplication by zero harmless.

If μ({x})=0 but μ({y})>0, use the positive-start formula at y, not x. Each relevant fiber contains y, so its mass is at least μ({y})>0. Every summand for a jump from y to x contains μ({x})=0, hence K(y,{x})=0. Both fluxes are again zero.

For an arbitrary kernel, a zero target atom does not imply K(y,{x})=0: that conclusion used the actual heat-bath transition law. Target-null starts may have nontrivial transition rules, but their outgoing flux is multiplied by zero.

On the two-bit cube, let μ give mass 1/2 to each of 00 and 11 and zero to the other states. Updating a single coordinate from either supported state leaves it unchanged. The kernel is reversible for μ, but 00 and 11 cannot communicate. Thus balance supplies neither irreducibility nor convergence from every start.

rubric.criterion: Separates the both-null and single-null cases without dividing by zero.
Uses the singleton formula at the positive-mass reverse start and proves fiber positivity.
Explains why an arbitrary kernel need not avoid a target-null atom.
Checks the 00/11 heat-bath counterexample and distinguishes reversibility from irreducibility.

cores.title: Adaptive hybrid error does not certify expected cost
assumptions: There are finitely many n adjacent hybrid pairs. At slot i the pair shares a probability law ρᵢ on histories, conditional Markov kernels Kᵢ,Lᵢ and a common downstream Markov kernel Sᵢ.

A measurable integrable real εᵢ bounds |Kᵢ(x,A)−Lᵢ(x,A)| for ρᵢ-almost every x and every measurable event A. Let βᵢ=∫εᵢ dρᵢ. Total variation means the supremum of absolute event-probability differences, with no extra factor of two.
cores.question: Derive an eventwise discrepancy bound Σᵢβᵢ between the first and last output laws. State why actual history laws and a fixed finite call range matter. Then refute the claim that vanishing TV distance alone transfers an unbounded expected query-cost bound.
steps: For each slot and fixed event A, Markov event probabilities are measurable and bounded by one, hence integrable under ρᵢ. Integrating the almost-everywhere conditional bound yields an averaged discrepancy at most βᵢ. The error function εᵢ is explicitly integrable; measurability of a supremum over all events was not assumed for free.

A common downstream Markov kernel preserves this uniform event bound by total-variation data processing. The same suffix must be used for the two members of the adjacent pair; otherwise that contraction argument is not applicable.

For a fixed final event A, telescope the n adjacent probability differences and use the triangle inequality: \[|P_n(A)-P_0(A)|\le\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\beta_i.\] Take the event supremum if desired. Each βᵢ uses its actual shared prefix-history law, not an unrelated ideal or proxy input law.

For integers N≥2 on the nonnegative reals, take μ_N=δ₀, ν_N=(1−1/N)δ₀+(1/N)δ_{N²} and c(x)=x. Then TV(μ_N,ν_N)=1/N→0, but E_{ν_N}c−E_{μ_N}c=N. All these individual expectations are finite; their gap is unbounded. A uniform cost bound, uniform integrability/tail control, or a separate actual-input cost analysis is needed.

A random recursion depth or stopping cap is not automatically this deterministic finite telescope. Its history construction, stopping/cap comparison, accumulated errors and actual-input expected cost remain separate obligations. This argument alone does not complete the Gaussian Cloud paper.

cores.title: A log-concave shape is not yet a probability density
assumptions: On ℝᵈ with d≥1 and Lebesgue reference measure, V is a finite real-valued Borel measurable convex function. Set ρ(x)=exp(−V(x)).
cores.question: Identify the log-concave shape and its logarithm. What additional numerical condition on Z=∫ρ(x)dx is required before ρ/Z defines a probability density? State which reference measure the word density refers to.
steps: The shape ρ is strictly positive and Borel measurable. Its logarithm is −V, a concave function by convexity of V, so this is a positive log-concave shape.
The normalizing quantity is \[Z=\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-V(x)}\,dx.\] A probability normalization requires 0<Z<∞, after which p(x)=ρ(x)/Z integrates to one against Lebesgue measure.

Log-concavity of the shape is a pointwise convex-analysis property; the finite integral is a separate analytic condition. This question asks to identify that obligation, not to prove that it holds for every convex potential.
For example V=0 has the log-concave shape ρ=1 but infinite Lebesgue integral on ℝᵈ. Thus the shape alone is not a normalized sampling target.

cores.title: Which space contains the sphere gradient?
assumptions: S is the unit sphere in ℝᵈ with d≥2, equipped with its induced Euclidean metric. A real-valued function f is smooth on a neighborhood of S. Let w∈S.
cores.question: Identify the tangent space at w and the defining directional-derivative identity for the gradient of f restricted to S. In what sense does this differ from the ambient Euclidean gradient? Do not prove an optimization convergence theorem.
steps: The tangent space is \[T_wS=\{v\in\mathbb R^d:\langle w,v\rangle=0\}.\] Its vectors are ambient vectors subject to an orthogonality condition.
The sphere gradient is the tangent vector G satisfying ⟨G,v⟩=Df(w)[v] for every v∈T_wS, using the induced inner product.

The ambient gradient represents derivatives in all ambient directions; it need not itself be tangent. Its orthogonal projection onto T_wS represents the same derivative on the allowed tangent directions.
This is the induced-metric sphere setting. Other manifolds and metrics need their own tangent spaces and gradient characterizations, not an automatic reuse of an ambient formula.

cores.title: What information does a coupling contain?

The independent product is a canonical feasible coupling: \[(\mu\otimes\nu)(A\times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B).\] Its marginals use the total masses equal to one.
Optimality requires a specified cost and a comparison of its integral over feasible plans. No optimality follows from the marginal identities alone.

cores.title: One random-site step is not one sweep
assumptions: The state space is a Boolean cube with m≥1 sites and target probability μ. For each site i, Kᵢ is the fixed coordinate heat-bath kernel, including its specified version on target-null fibers.
cores.question: Describe one uniform random-scan step and its mixture kernel. How does that time unit differ from a sweep of all sites? Does the mixture-law description itself specify a mixing time or an oracle-query cost?
steps: One step first chooses one site I uniformly among the m sites, then draws the new state with kernel K_I, retaining the other coordinates.
The transition law is the state-independent mixture \[K(x,A)=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^{m}K_i(x,A).\] A coordinate resampling may return its previous value, so an update need not change the state.
A sweep applies coordinate updates across all sites according to a specified schedule; it is not this single random-site kernel step. Comparing bounds requires the same time convention.

A noncomputable transition-law definition alone supplies neither an implemented conditional sampler, its query cost, nor a mixing-time estimate. Those guarantees require additional algorithmic and analytic results.

cores.title: Invariant, reversible and convergent are different claims
assumptions: P is a finite row-stochastic transition matrix: P(x,y)≥0 and Σ_y P(x,y)=1. π and ρ are probability row vectors. Use total variation when discussing convergence.
cores.question: Write the identities defining invariance and detailed balance for π. State what convergence from ρ means in this setting. Which identity controls one step started exactly in π, and why is that not the definition of convergence from an arbitrary start?
steps: Invariance is πP=π, or Σ_x π(x)P(x,y)=π(y) for each y. Starting exactly in π therefore gives the same law after one step.

Convergence from ρ is \[\operatorname{TV}(\rho P^t,\pi)\longrightarrow0\quad(t\to\infty).\] It concerns an entire sequence of laws from the specified start, not just the identity πP=π.
For the identity matrix P, every π is invariant and reversible, but ρP^t=ρ for all t. If ρ≠π, convergence to π fails. Thus one-step invariance is not a definition of general-start convergence.

cores.title: A quadratic gradient through the actual sphere differential
assumptions: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space with \(\dim E=n+1\), where \(n\in\mathbb N\). Let \(S=\{x\in E:\|x\|=1\}\) have its standard smooth sphere structure.
\(A:E\to E\) is a symmetric continuous linear map and \(q(y)=\langle y,Ay\rangle\). Fix \(x\in S\), let \(i:S\hookrightarrow E\) be the actual inclusion, and put \(K=(\mathbb R x)^\perp\).
Tangent directions \(w\in T_xS\) are paired through \(D i_x w\in K\) using the ambient inner product. No default inner product on chart coordinates is identified with this induced pairing.
cores.question: For every z in K, prove that D(q restricted to S)_x(w)=⟨D i_x(w),z⟩ for all w in T_xS if and only if z=2(Ax−⟨x,Ax⟩x). Justify the ambient derivative, the unit-normal projection and the uniqueness direction. Use genuine differentiability, not the totalized derivative's fallback value.
steps: Symmetry gives the genuine ambient derivative \[Dq_x(v)=\langle v,Ax\rangle+\langle x,Av\rangle=2\langle v,Ax\rangle.\] Hence the real gradient is \(g=2Ax\). The bounded linear map and quadratic operations supply differentiability; the equality is not an inference from a totalized zero derivative.

For the actual inclusion, \(\operatorname{range}(D i_x)=K\). The chain rule therefore gives \[D(q|_S)_x(w)=\langle D i_x(w),g\rangle.\] This uses the inclusion-induced pairing, not an assumed isometry from an arbitrary chart metric.
Because \(\|x\|=1\), orthogonal projection onto K satisfies \[P_Ku=u-\langle x,u\rangle x.\] Substituting g yields the tangent vector \[G=P_K(2Ax)=2(Ax-\langle x,Ax\rangle x).\]

Every \(D i_x(w)\) lies in K, so orthogonal projection preserves its pairing with g. Thus G represents the restricted differential. Conversely, if a tangent vector z has the same pairing for every w, surjectivity onto K makes \(z-G\) orthogonal to every vector in K. Taking its inner product with itself gives \(z=G\), proving the equivalence.

cores.title: Averaging a conditional event-error bound
assumptions: \(A,B\) are arbitrary measurable spaces, \(\mu\) is a probability measure on A, and \(K,L:A\leadsto B\) are Markov kernels.

\(\varepsilon:A\to\mathbb R\) is integrable under μ. On one common μ-full-measure set of inputs x, every measurable event s satisfies \[|K(x,s)-L(x,s)|\le\varepsilon(x).\] Event masses in this inequality are finite real probabilities.
cores.question: For every measurable event t, prove |(K composed with μ)(t)−(L composed with μ)(t)|≤∫ε dμ. Give the measurability, finiteness and integrability justifications required to subtract the two real integrals and use almost-everywhere domination. Do not assume a measurable total-variation supremum or a query-cost conclusion.
steps: Fix a measurable event t. Kernel measurability makes \(k_t(x)=K(x,t)\) and \(l_t(x)=L(x,t)\) measurable real functions. Markov normalization gives \(0\le k_t,l_t\le1\); since μ is a probability measure, both are integrable.

The bind/composition law gives \[(K\circ_m\mu)(t)=\int k_t\,d\mu,\qquad(L\circ_m\mu)(t)=\int l_t\,d\mu.\] In Lean the underlying masses are extended nonnegative reals. Their finiteness, supplied by the probability-kernel assumptions, justifies conversion to real integrals; the totalized toReal API is not used as if infinity were finite.

The two integrable event functions can be subtracted inside the integral. The integral triangle inequality gives \[\left|\int k_t\,d\mu-\int l_t\,d\mu\right|\le\int|k_t-l_t|\,d\mu.\] The absolute difference is integrable as well.

The common almost-everywhere hypothesis supplies \(|k_t-l_t|\le\varepsilon\) almost everywhere for this event. Monotonicity for integrable real functions yields \[|(K\circ_m\mu)(t)-(L\circ_m\mu)(t)|\le\int\varepsilon\,d\mu.\] No measurable supremum over all events is needed, and no new global nonnegativity premise on ε is inserted.

rubric.criterion: Establishes event measurability and boundedness by one, hence integrability under the probability input law.
Uses the bind law with finite event masses to justify the real expectation identities.
Justifies integral subtraction and the triangle inequality using integrability, not a formal subtraction of infinities.
Applies the common almost-everywhere event bound and integrability of ε without assuming a measurable TV supremum or an expected-cost theorem.

cores.title: Gluing the right joint law before applying Minkowski
assumptions: \(E\) is a nonempty normed additive commutative group, with its Borel measurable structure, second-countable topology and a standard Borel measurable space. No vector-space or finite-dimensional structure is assumed.

\(\mu_1,\mu_2,\mu_3\) are probability measures on E. Couplings have exactly the two prescribed coordinate marginals. Define \[C(\gamma)=\left(\int\|x-y\|^2\,d\gamma(x,y)\right)^{1/2}.\] Both costs and \(W_2\) take values in \([0,\infty]\); \(W_2\) is the square root of the infimum of squared coupling costs.

The external thresholds \(r_{12},r_{23}\in[0,\infty]\) satisfy \[W_2(\mu_1,\mu_2)<r_{12},\qquad W_2(\mu_2,\mu_3)<r_{23}.\] Neither optimal-plan existence nor finite individual second moments is given.
cores.question: Prove \(W_2(\mu_1,\mu_3)<r_{12}+r_{23}\) by choosing strictly near-optimal adjacent plans and gluing them over their common middle marginal. Identify the measure used in Minkowski, justify all three pair-marginal cost identities and explain the measurability/conditional-version requirements. Audit the shortcut \(\Gamma'=\gamma_{12}\otimes\mu_3\): use identical Bernoulli marginals and diagonal adjacent plans to show exactly which identification fails. Do not assume optimal-plan attainment or convert extended costs to real numbers.
steps: Strict near-optimal selection gives actual couplings \(\gamma_{12},\gamma_{23}\) with \[C(\gamma_{12})<r_{12},\qquad C(\gamma_{23})<r_{23}.\] These are consequences of the transport infimum and positive square-root order, not an assumption that the infimum is attained. A coupling of a probability marginal has total mass one, so both plans are probability measures.

Disintegrate the second plan with respect to its first coordinate. The finite standard-Borel conditional-kernel theorem supplies a Markov version \(\kappa(y,dz)\) with \[\gamma_{23}(dy,dz)=\mu_2(dy)\kappa(y,dz).\] Define \[\Gamma(d(x,y),dz)=\gamma_{12}(dx,dy)\kappa(y,dz).\] Markov normalization preserves its first pair marginal. Equality \(\gamma_{12}.\mathrm{snd}=\mu_2=\gamma_{23}.\mathrm{fst}\), kernel measurability and the disintegration identity preserve the second pair marginal. Conditional representatives need only have the correct \(\mu_2\)-almost-everywhere meaning; an unsupported pointwise conditional formula is not used.

Write \(\pi_{ij}\) for the measurable pair projections from the same triple space. The identities are \[(\pi_{12})_\#\Gamma=\gamma_{12},\qquad(\pi_{23})_\#\Gamma=\gamma_{23}.\] Put \(\gamma_{13}=(\pi_{13})_\#\Gamma\). Composing measurable coordinate projections proves that its marginals are \(\mu_1,\mu_3\). The Borel norm and the product/projection measurability justify nonnegative pushforward integration; no subtraction of infinite integrals occurs.

For \(e_{ij}(x,y,z)=\|x_i-x_j\|\), all edge functions are measurable. Nonnegative pushforward integration gives \[\|e_{12}\|_{L^2(\Gamma)}=C(\gamma_{12}),\qquad\|e_{23}\|_{L^2(\Gamma)}=C(\gamma_{23}).\] The endpoint identity is \[\|e_{13}\|_{L^2(\Gamma)}=C(\gamma_{13}).\] Pointwise \(e_{13}\le e_{12}+e_{23}\) and extended-nonnegative L² Minkowski apply on this single law Γ, not on two unrelated pair spaces.

Using the endpoint coupling to bound the infimum, then the preceding identities, yields \[\begin{aligned}W_2(\mu_1,\mu_3)&\le C(\gamma_{13})\\&\le C(\gamma_{12})+C(\gamma_{23})\\&<r_{12}+r_{23}.\end{aligned}\] The coefficient is exactly one on each cost. Strict extended-order addition handles the thresholds without an infinity-minus-infinity operation. No optimal plan, density or individual second-moment assumption is added.

For the shortcut audit, take \(E=\mathbb R\) and all three marginals equal to \(\frac12\delta_0+\frac12\delta_1\), with both adjacent plans diagonal. Their costs are zero. Under \(\Gamma'=\gamma_{12}\otimes\mu_3\), Y and Z are independent, so \[\mathbb P_{\Gamma'}(Y\ne Z)=\tfrac12,\qquad\|e_{23}\|_{L^2(\Gamma')}=1/\sqrt2.\] Its second pair marginal is the independent product, not the diagonal \(\gamma_{23}\), and cannot have cost zero. This refutes the shortcut's cost identification, not the true Wasserstein inequality. Correct conditional gluing makes X=Y=Z in this example.

cores.title: Why a global Lipschitz function bounds its supporting vectors
assumptions: E is a real inner-product space, not necessarily complete or finite dimensional. The function f:E→ℝ is globally G-Lipschitz, where G≥0.

A supplied vector g supports f at x globally: \[f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\le f(y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E.\] Existence of supporting vectors, convexity of f and differentiability are not additional premises.
cores.question: Prove \(\|g\|\le G\), making the test point and zero case explicit. Is the same conclusion valid if the support inequality holds only for y in a constraint set C containing x? Give a counterexample with a globally Lipschitz function and explain exactly which step no longer applies.
steps: Because the support relation is global, its test point may be y=x+g. Thus \[\|g\|^2=\langle g,g\rangle\le f(x+g)-f(x).\] This tests the supplied relation; it does not use a theorem constructing subgradients.
Global Lipschitz growth and the absolute-value bound give \[f(x+g)-f(x)\le|f(x+g)-f(x)|\le G\|g\|.\] Combining the inequalities yields \(\|g\|^2\le G\|g\|\).

If g=0 the conclusion is immediate from G≥0. Otherwise \(\|g\|>0\), so division by this strictly positive number gives \(\|g\|\le G\). No completeness, differentiability or finite-dimensional compactness is used.

For constrained support take E=ℝ, f≡0, G=0, C=[0,∞), x=0 and g=−1. Then \[f(0)+g(y-0)=-y\le0=f(y)\qquad(y\in C),\] but \(\|g\|=1>0=G\). The chosen point x+g=−1 is outside C. This refutes the constrained variant, not the globally quantified theorem.

Expanding the actual update in the inner-product space gives \[\|x_{k+1}-z\|^2=\|x_k-z\|^2-2a_k\langle g_k,x_k-z\rangle+a_k^2\|g_k\|^2.\] Since aₖ≥0, multiplication preserves the support inequality; since aₖ²≥0, the norm bound gives \[2a_k(f(x_k)-f(z))\le\|x_k-z\|^2-\|x_{k+1}-z\|^2+G^2a_k^2.\] A negative step would invalidate the first inference.

Sum these finite inequalities; the distance terms telescope exactly: \[2\sum_{k<N}a_k(f(x_k)-f(z))\le\|x_0-z\|^2+G^2\sum_{k<N}a_k^2-\|x_N-z\|^2.\] This statement permits zero steps and N=0. It retains, rather than assumes away, the nonnegative terminal distance.

For N>0 choose i minimizing f(xₖ) over the finite nonempty index set {0,…,N−1}. This is a finite minimum, not existence of a global minimizer of f. Put \(A=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}a_k>0\). Positive weights imply \[A(f(x_i)-f(z))\le\sum_{k<N}a_k(f(x_k)-f(z)).\] Drop the nonpositive terminal term from the upper bound and divide by 2A>0 to obtain the requested ratio.

When a=R/(G√N)>0, the ratio is at most \[\frac{R^2+G^2Na^2}{2Na}=\frac{R^2}{2Na}+\frac{G^2a}{2}=\frac{RG}{\sqrt N}.\] The chosen schedule depends on N; this does not establish that one fixed infinite run uses all these horizon-dependent schedules simultaneously.

At N=0 the energy inequality reduces to 0≤0, but there is no i<0 and division by a zero sum cannot create one (Lean's totalized 0/0 does not repair existence). If R=0 then z=x₀ and, for N>0, i=0 already has zero gap. If G=0 global Lipschitz growth makes f constant and the norm lemma forces all supplied gₖ=0; the positive-parameter step formula is unnecessary. These degenerate cases are separate arguments, not a substitution into a formula requiring positive parameters.

cores.title: Why retaining one coordinate and conditionally resampling the other is invariant
assumptions: α and β are measurable spaces; β is nonempty and standard Borel. μ is any finite nonnegative measure on α×β, including the zero measure. No standard-Borel or nonempty assumption is imposed on α.

Let μ₁ be the first marginal and κ(a,db) a selected measurable regular conditional Markov kernel for the second coordinate given the first. You may use the existing finite-measure disintegration identity \[\mu(da,db)=\mu_1(da)\kappa(a,db).\] Its conditional characterization is only μ₁-almost everywhere; the selected version has mass one at every input.
The actual update retains a and resamples b: \[K((a,b),d(a',b'))=\delta_a(da')\kappa(a,db').\] Invariant means the measure equality μK=μ, not convergence from every starting measure.
cores.question: Prove μK=μ by identifying the measure after projecting to the retained coordinate and after applying the product kernel. Explain the role of measurability, the finite-measure disintegration, and the chosen conditional version on null fibers. Must μ be a probability measure? Give a finite-state example showing why this invariance result alone does not imply convergence from another initial probability law.
steps: The deterministic projection (a,b)↦a is measurable. Pushing μ through it gives exactly its first marginal \(\mu_1=(\mathrm{fst})_\#\mu\). This assertion uses the actual input μ, not an arbitrary starting law with a different first marginal.

The product kernel a↦δₐ⊗κ(a,·) is measurable because it is the product of the identity kernel and the measurable conditional kernel. Composition with the deterministic projection gives K. Associativity of kernel/measure composition yields \[\mu K=\mu_1(\mathrm{id}\times\kappa)=\mu_1\otimes\kappa.\] The last expression is a measure–kernel composition product, not the independent product of μ₁ and a fixed marginal.

The supplied finite-measure disintegration identity now gives \[\mu K=\mu_1\otimes\kappa=\mu.\] It is justified by the standard-Borel, nonempty β and finite μ interface. No density, positivity, normalization to mass one or division by a marginal density is required. For μ=0 both sides are zero; this is invariant as a finite measure, not a probability law.

Conditional versions agree in their prescribed conditional meaning only for μ₁-almost every a. Replacing them on a μ₁-null set does not change the integrated identity. The chosen global Markov version still yields a legitimate mass-one update there, but no claim about conditional support or convergence from such exceptional starting states follows.

For lack of convergence take α={0,1}, β={∗} with discrete measurable structures and \(\mu=(\tfrac12\delta_0+\tfrac12\delta_1)\otimes\delta_\ast\). The update never changes either coordinate, so K is the identity kernel. Starting from \(\rho=\delta_{(0,\ast)}\), \[\rho K^n=\rho,\qquad d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\rho K^n,\mu)=\tfrac12\quad(n\ge0).\] Thus the actual invariant target does not imply uniqueness, irreducibility, mixing or convergence from a different first marginal.

cores.title: One null set for every event, or a different null set for each event?
assumptions: Ω is an uncountable set equipped with the countable/co-countable σ-algebra: a measurable set is countable or has countable complement. Define μ(B)=0 for countable B and μ(B)=1 for co-countable B. Both input and output spaces use this σ-algebra.

For measurable B define K(x,B)=1_B(x) and L(x,B)=μ(B). A Markov kernel must be a probability measure in B for each x, and measurable in x for every measurable B. The total-variation event supremum is not assumed measurable.

Compare the statements \[(\forall B\text{ measurable})\;(K(x,B)=L(x,B)\text{ for }\mu\text{-a.e. }x)\] and \[\mu\text{-a.e. }x\;(\forall B\text{ measurable})\;K(x,B)=L(x,B).\] In the second statement the same exceptional set must work for all events.
cores.question: Verify that μ is a probability measure and K,L are measurable Markov kernels. Prove the first quantified statement but refute the second. Compute both output laws after averaging over μ: does this example refute equality of the averaged laws? Explain exactly what it does—and does not—show about the uniform eventwise hypothesis in the local conditional-error bound, and why it is not a standard-Borel counterexample.
steps: Uncountability ensures a set cannot be both countable and co-countable, so μ is well defined, with μ(Ω)=1 and μ(∅)=0. For a disjoint sequence of measurable sets, if one is co-countable, all the others are countable and their union is co-countable; the sum and union mass are one. If none is co-countable, the countable union is countable and both masses are zero. This proves countable additivity.

For each x, K(x,·)=δₓ and L(x,·)=μ are probability measures. For each fixed measurable B, x↦K(x,B)=1_B(x) is measurable and x↦L(x,B)=μ(B) is constant. Hence both assignments are Markov kernels; no diagonal-subset measurability in the product space is asserted or needed.

If B is countable, L(x,B)=0 and K differs only on the μ-null set B. If B is co-countable, L(x,B)=1 and K differs only on its μ-null complement. Thus \[\forall B\text{ measurable},\qquad K(\cdot,B)=L(\cdot,B)\quad\mu\text{-a.e.}\] The exceptional set depends on B.

For every x choose the measurable singleton B={x}. Then \[K(x,\{x\})=1,\qquad L(x,\{x\})=0.\] Consequently no x has equality for all measurable events. There cannot be a common full-measure set. An uncountable union of the individual null exceptions may be all of Ω; countable closure of null sets does not justify that union.

Nevertheless, for each measurable B, \[(\mu K)(B)=\int 1_B(x)\,d\mu(x)=\mu(B),\qquad(\mu L)(B)=\int\mu(B)\,d\mu=\mu(B).\] Both output measures are μ. This refutes the quantifier interchange and equality of kernel versions almost everywhere, not the true averaged-law equality. For a fixed output event an averaging proof can use that event's own exceptional set; a common null set is a sufficient stronger API premise, not shown mathematically necessary for the averaged conclusion.

The output σ-algebra here is not countably generated: any countable family of countable/co-countable generators involves a countable union C of their countable sides, and every generator is constant on Ω∖C. Every generated measurable set is therefore constant there, but the full σ-algebra contains a singleton inside Ω∖C and can separate it from another such point. The uncountable input also is not a countable type. Thus this is outside the countable-input-or-countably-generated-output interface used by Mathlib's finite-kernel uniqueness theorem. Standard-Borel outputs have countably generated σ-algebras; this example does not refute that theorem or the selected conditional-distribution interface.
